1. The perceived impact on the local community – whether positive or negative 2. The perceived presence or absence of local participation – motivators and deterrents such as existing

barriers to entry in the industry

To achieve the aims outlined, this study will also need to investigate the wider context of the French Polynesian recreational dive industry – information about which seems to be lacking in current literature. Hence, in the following protocol I highlight the procedure I followed to gather some preliminary information about the demographics of recreational scuba dive clubs in French Polynesia

Several limitations are important. We do not claim that eigendirections exhaust all critical points of Lρ; in dimension two, deletion leaves a pure state and the landscape is constant. The finitedimensional PEDL calculus is proved directly. The Marchenko–Pastur outlier kernel is deterministic conditional on Stieltjes-transform convergence. In the spiked covariance section, the compactly subcritical tilted spectral-measure limit is derived by importing standard anisotropic local laws rather than reproving them from scratch; the resulting PEDL coefficient theorem is stated away from the BBP edges and from the hard lower-edge regime γ = 1. We also do not claim that PEDL is a sharp BBP threshold test. The main spiked-model conclusion is smoother and more geometric: below BBP, the top-eigenvector overlap vanishes but the spike-direction spectral measure has a tilted bulk footprint; near threshold, finite edge components can be visible at finite dimension. Relation to prior work

The spectral calculations use classical Cauchy interlacing, rank-one compression, secular equations, and matrix perturbation theory [10, 14, 15, 17]. Those tools explain how the eigenvalues of a rank-one compression move; the new object here is the entropy functional placed on that motion. In particular, the Morse coefficients and Cauchy-root transport formulas below are not new secular equations, but new entropy-deletion consequences of them. The scalar motivation is adjacent to Shannon entropy, R´enyi entropy, information spectrum, large deviations, f-divergences, and information-loss viewpoints [1, 3, 11–13, 19, 24, 26]. Effective rank and matrix entropy give scalar summaries of spectral spread [25]. PEDL differs from these scalar summaries by retaining the projective direction that is deleted before entropy is evaluated. The high-dimensional sections sit within the random-matrix and statistical-mechanics tradition of spectral measures, deterministic equivalents, and eigenvalue phase transitions [2, 21, 22]. More specifically, they use Marchenko–Pastur theory and spiked covariance asymptotics [4–8, 16, 20, 23, 27]. The diagonal-resolvent interpretation is standard in isotropic and anisotropic local-law frameworks for sample covariance matrices [9, 18]. The tilted spectral measure itself should therefore be read as a deterministic-equivalent consequence, not as an independent local law proved from scratch here. The contribution is the passage from that direction-specific spectral measure to a finite-dimensional entropy-deletion landscape and to the corresponding effective-rank-normalized PEDL coefficient. This positioning also separates the present work from optimal testing theory for known-direction alternatives. When the candidate direction and sign are known, linear statistics such as v∗SNv, signed rank contrasts, and tuned power moments can use the first-order signed part of the tilted measure. PEDL is instead an unsigned von Neumann deletion-geometry contrast. Its value in the spiked model is not that it dominates these linear procedures, but that it gives an entropy-geometric functional whose limit is governed by the same tilted projective spectral measure. Thus the randommatrix portion should be read as a proof-of-principle limit theorem for a new landscape functional, not as a replacement for the classical locally optimized linear-statistic viewpoint.

## 13 Discussion

Projective entropy deletion turns spectral entropy into a geometric response field. The finitedimensional theory shows that eigendirections carry computable Morse data, and the first-variation theory shows that perturbations move entropy through Cauchy-root transport. The Marchenko– Pastur theorem identifies an infinitesimal outlier response as a Stieltjes-transform contour functional, not as the scalar atom kernel. The contrast-family viewpoint sharpens the interpretation of the spiked covariance results. PEDL is the von Neumann/deletion member of a broader family of contrasts between the candidatedirection spectral measure and the MP reference law. Linear signed contrasts record the first-order direction of the tilt; divergence and PEDL-type contrasts record its magnitude. The candidatedirection test shows that the PEDL magnitude has finite-sample inferential value relative to an

Scalar entropy deletion reveals shells. Projective spectral deletion reveals transport. In spiked models, transport interacts with the spike-direction spectral measure. Below threshold, this measure is tilted across the bulk; near threshold, finite edge components are visible but do not exhaust the signal. PEDL is sensitive to this projective measure rather than only to an outlier coordinate. The candidate-direction experiment shows that this sensitivity is not just descriptive: it yields a finite-sample calibrated entropy-deletion statistic with high subcritical power in settings where an empirical largest-eigenvalue test remains near the null level. This should not be read as an optimality statement for known-direction testing; the contrast-family analysis identifies linear and tuned power statistics as natural competitors and companions. The strongest theorem-level results are finite-dimensional: the Cauchy-root formula, exact entropy identity, Morse-Hessian theorem, first variation, and contour transport. The high-dimensional theorem is compactly subcritical: after importing standard anisotropic local laws for spiked sample covariance matrices, Theorems 10.1 and 10.8 identify the tilted projective spectral measure and the PEDL coefficient away from the BBP edges and away from the hard lower-edge regime. The numerical simulations show that the finite-p coefficients already track this deterministic object closely. The threshold-uniform theorem and the full supercritical bulk-plus-outlier PEDL limit remain open problems.

## 7 Limitations and outlook

Detection below the threshold

Theorem 3.2 sharpens, rather than contradicts, the known fact that subcritical spikes are detectable from the bulk spectrum [30, 16]: detection succeeds despite perfect analyticity, not because of any singularity — the signal is the O(1) mean shift of Proposition 6.1 against O(1) Gaussian fluctuations, and the transition manifests only as the logarithmic divergence of the accumulated information, at the exact rate given by the local energy (Corollary 6.3).

Open problems

(1) Beyond Gaussian invariant fluctuations: Corollaries 3.12 and 3.14 prove fluctuation-level analytic invisibility for the canonical Gaussian invariant ensembles. The next probabilistic problem is non-Gaussian universality, including the model-dependent N−1 bias and higher cumulant corrections, and the finer N−1/3 BBP critical window. K-FAC is computationally attractive because storage, inversion, and damping can exploit Kronecker identities [9]. Convolutional K-FAC adapts the same idea to shared filters [4]; modern K-FAC frameworks extend it to generic linear weight-sharing layers [2]. Several prior variants improve K-FAC without making the residual itself the central object. EKFAC/KFEstyle methods correct diagonal variances in the Kronecker-factored eigenbasis [3]. K-FOC formulates the problem of finding optimal Kronecker factors as a best rank-one approximation problem [12]. This paper is complementary: we use best rank-one Kronecker factors and KFE-style diagonal correction as baselines, but focus on the residual beyond standard K-FAC and on the decision consequences of that residual.

## 3 Experimental program and validity design

The experimental design is organized so that each experiment tries to falsify a simpler explanation of the residual.

Controlled MLPs. Controlled width and activation sweeps test whether κ decays away as finite-width noise. It does not over the tested widths. Best-rank-one experiments test whether standard K-FAC is merely the unavoidable rank-one Kronecker approximation. It is not: better rank-one factors consistently improve on standard K-FAC.

Low-rank residual spectrum. Oracle residual-SVD experiments test whether the residual is compressible in Kronecker-product coordinates. These oracle experiments are upper bounds: they use the evaluation residual and are not deployable methods. They show what is structurally possible.

External validity and curvature type. The external-validity gate was a robustness gate across synthetic regression, non-Gaussian tabular regression, binary classification, and patch-level convolutional diagnostics. The real-data exact-block study then used stronger public-data blocks: diabetes regression, breast-cancer classification, digits 3-vs-8 MLPs, and exact tied-filter convolutional blocks. Empirical-Fisher and GGN-style blocks are both evaluated to avoid over-reliance on empirical-Fisher artifacts. The external-validity gate is treated as a gate and audit trail; the real-data exact-block study is the primary external-validity evidence used for claims.

Non-oracle transfer. The regularized transfer study uses train/fit/validation/evaluation splits to fit residual dictionaries without using the evaluation residual. This design deliberately distinguishes oracle repairability from practical correction.

Decision consequences. The broad-grid study tests broad candidate model grids under a single-block Laplace evidence proxy. The near-boundary benchmark then targets near-tie pairwise evidence decisions mined from the broad-grid study and rerun prospectively over new seeds and train fractions.

### 4.2 The residual does not decay over controlled widths

In trained controlled MLPs, standard K-FAC residuals remain around 0.36–0.37 from width 8 to width 1024 (Table 4; Figure 2). The residual mildly increases over the tested range rather than vanishing. In the controlled grid, the activation ordering linear < tanh < SiLU < GELU < ReLU holds in nearly all paired comparisons, indicating that activation/Jacobian structure contributes to the residual.

### 4.3 The residual is low-Kronecker-rank compressible

The strongest structural result is residual compressibility. In the nonlinear controlled low-rank residual study grid, rank 16 captures about 0.88 of residual energy, rank 32 about 0.94, and rank 64 about 0.97 (Table 5; Figure 3). Rank scaling still grows with width: k90, k95, and k99 have mean power exponents around 0.77, 0.81, and 0.88, respectively. Thus the result is not a fixed finite-rank theorem; it is a finite-width compressibility law with rank growth. This rank growth has a natural interpretation from Eq. 3. After Kronecker rearrangement, the residual rank is the rank, or effective rank, of a cross-covariance operator between activation outer-product features and backpropagated-gradient outer-product features. A useful scaling conjecture is therefore that the Kronecker rank needed to capture a fixed residual-energy fraction grows like k1−ρ(d) ≍dαρ, where d is width and αρ is controlled by the number of activation–gradient covariance modes that remain shared at that energy threshold. Under approximately Gaussian preactivations, the activation side is naturally organized by the Hermite expansion of the nonlinearity; slower Hermite-coefficient decay should create more persistent activation-side covariance modes and therefore larger finite-width effective rank. The measured exponents 0.77/0.81/0.88 for 90%/95%/99% energy capture and the observed activation ordering are consistent with this picture, but we treat it as a phenomenological scaling law rather than a theorem. A direct Hermite-order decomposition of saved residual factors would be the sharper test.

### 4.4 Mode alignment supports mechanism, not noise

The mode-alignment studies show that leading residual directions align with structured dictionaries. For nonlinear controlled MLPs, the leading A-side residual factor has mean Hermite alignment 0.94. The simple B-side dictionary is weak, but enriched weighted-input features raise top-mode B-side alignment from 0.17 to 0.77 on average (Table 6). This supports a mechanism picture rather than arbitrary dense noise.

## 5 External validity: the residual survives real data and GGN checks

The real-data exact-block study uses public-data snapshots and an exact tied-filter convolutional block. The residual persists across real tabular regression, real tabular classification, digits MLP, and exact tied convolution, under both empirical-Fisher and GGN-style curvature (Table 7; Figure 4). Nonlinear standard K-FAC residuals are large in all four families. Rank-32 oracle correction captures nearly all residual energy in several real-data MLP settings and remains highly effective in exact tied convolution. The empirical-Fisher limitation is addressed directly. Cross-curvature agreement between empirical-Fisher and GGN standard K-FAC residual sizes is high in three of four families and strong overall (Table 8). The real-digits MLP is the weakest family but still has positive agreement. The main residual claim therefore does not rest solely on empirical-Fisher behavior. The real-data results motivate a three-mechanism taxonomy. First, nonlinear activations and Jacobians create residual structure in controlled regression. Second, data-dependent curvature weighting creates residuals even for linear classification models, because probabilities or residuals depend on inputs. Third, tied filters create spatial cross-position correlations that standard convolutional K-FAC misses.

### 8.1 Prospective near-tie design

The near-boundary benchmark mines a frozen manifest of 60 pair regimes from the completed broad-grid evidence metrics and reruns them prospectively over held-out seeds and train fractions. The manifest contains 24 high-risk near-tie pairs, 12 observed-flip replays, 12 low-risk near-tie controls, and 12 obvious-decision controls. The central diagnostic is the realized danger score

Each run records exact, standard K-FAC, best-rank-one, KFE/EKFAC-style diagonal, oracle residual, fit-SVD, and random correction rows. Validation passes with 360/360 job files and 124,964 rows. The design deliberately includes controls that should not flip. A useful outcome is therefore not simply a high flip rate; it is separation between obvious decisions and near-boundary decisions, plus repair by methods that use true residual structure.

### 8.2 Obvious decisions are stable; near-boundary decisions flip

Standard K-FAC produces 115 flips in 3064 near-boundary pairwise rows, a 3.75% overall flip rate. The bucket breakdown is the key result (Table 16; Figure 7). Obvious controls have 0/472 flips despite large absolute margin errors, because their exact margins are enormous. Near-tie buckets have nontrivial flip rates: 4.86% in high-risk near-tie, 4.32% in low-risk near-tie controls, and 3.70% in observed-flip replay. Thus the pre-mined high-risk label is not a perfect prospective predictor; near-boundary structure itself is the robust failure regime. This is an important refinement of the research claim. The mined high-risk bucket was designed to concentrate fragile cases, but the realized evidence is more precise: any pair can be safe if its realized margin is large, and any near-tie pair can be fragile if the realized differential approximation error is comparable to that margin. Exact-margin deciles sharpen the same point (Table 17; Figure 8). The smallest exact-margin decile flips 19.87% of the time, the second decile 7.19%, and larger-margin deciles rapidly approach zero. K-FAC is not globally decision-unstable; it is boundary-fragile. The realized danger score is the strongest mechanism-level oracle diagnostic (Table 18; Figure 9). Bins below one have no flips; bins above one have elevated flip rates; the 10–50 bin flips 33.33% of the time. This validates the algebraic principle that approximation error matters when it is large relative to the exact margin. The threshold diagnostic in Table 19 makes the circularity explicit: danger > 1 is necessary for every observed flip in this benchmark, but it is far from sufficient, giving 100% recall and only 10.5% precision. Thus the danger score is best interpreted as an oracle mechanism check, not as the deployable contribution.

## 9 Synthesis: novelty, significance, and application

The final evidence supports a focused submission claim.

Novelty. The novel object is not just the K-FAC residual; it is the decision-local failure mode induced by that residual. Boundary fragility asks whether curvature-approximation error is large relative to the evidence margin and aligned in the direction that changes the decision. This reframes approximate-curvature evaluation from global reconstruction accuracy to decision reliability.

Significance. Approximate Laplace evidence can look stable on broad grids while still failing in the regime where evidence is most needed: close comparisons. The broad-grid and near-boundary studies together show why large absolute evidence distortion is neither necessary nor sufficient as a decision-risk statement. The important variable is differential error divided by margin. That principle should transfer beyond standard K-FAC to other approximate curvature methods used for scalable Bayesian deep learning.

Application. The application result today is an audit-oriented warning signal, not a solved correction method. The Boundary Fragility Score uses K-FAC-side margin and effective-dimension quantities to flag near-boundary comparisons that should be audited, refined, or abstained from; nested ablations show that effective-dimension features add signal beyond approximate margin alone. KFE/EKFAC-style diagonal correction is a meaningful partial repair, while oracle rank-32 correction shows that the missing signal is structured and repairable. Practical residual-aware correction remains open.

Non-claims. A width-specific Occam-bias headline is not supported. The existing data support an effectivedimension directionality result but do not support the stronger claim that K-FAC systematically favors narrower networks near evidence boundaries. Full-network marginal likelihood and posterior predictive consequences are also not yet established.

## 10 Limitations

Single-block Laplace proxy. The evidence score isolates one exact block’s curvature contribution. This is scientifically useful because it directly tests the residual’s consequence, but it is not a full-network marginal likelihood. A full-network Laplace calculation could either amplify these errors, if multiple blocks shift the same decision boundary, or partially cancel them, if block errors have opposite signs. A sharper conditional hypothesis follows from the directionality results: if per-block signed evidence biases are sign-consistent and effective-dimension orderings correlate across layers, differential errors can add coherently across blocks while exact margins add less coherently, making the danger ratio grow with block count. Testing cross-block sign correlation and cross-layer effective-dimension ordering is therefore the key full-network follow-up. The present claim remains block-level and boundary-local, not a claim about end-to-end Bayesian model selection at scale.

Small-to-moderate exact blocks. Exact curvature blocks are necessarily small enough to construct and decompose. The results motivate larger architectural probes, especially transformer and other weight-sharing blocks, but do not by themselves prove behavior at modern scale.

Empirical-Fisher tail. The empirical-Fisher real-digits MLP tail is computationally hard. The regularizedtransfer study had 19 missing cells under the original configuration. The near-boundary benchmark completed all jobs, but the final 22 jobs used an ultralight completion configuration, all in the empirical-Fisher realdigits MLP obvious-control stratum. Since those rows are obvious-decision controls, the high-risk near-tie conclusions are unaffected, but full-method coverage in that control stratum is reduced. The repeated location of the difficulty is itself informative: the failures concentrate in dense empirical-Fisher digits-MLP blocks where repeated logdet/eigensolve/dictionary-validation operations are most ill-conditioned. We therefore interpret the tail as an empirical-Fisher numerical-fragility stratum and keep GGN-style results as the cleaner primary curvature check.

This is a limitation of both result and design: the near-boundary flips are samewidth activation comparisons, while the width-difference rows are obvious controls. A future experiment should deliberately construct near-tie width-comparison pairs before claiming or rejecting width-dependent marginal-likelihood bias.

No posterior-predictive endpoint yet. The decision studies evaluate evidence scores and evidenceboundary decisions, not posterior predictive calibration, Brier score, or test NLL under full Laplace sampling. The next consequence experiment should evaluate posterior predictive uncertainty precisely at the boundary cases identified here.

Practical correction remains unresolved. Oracle residual correction proves repairability; it is not deployable. KFE helps and should be a serious baseline. Fit-SVD and random dictionaries do not yet provide a robust practical solution.

## 11 Broader impact, ethics, and AI assistance disclosure

Broader impact. This work is primarily a diagnostic study of approximate curvature reliability. Its positive impact is to make approximate Bayesian evidence pipelines more auditable: a model-selection or prior-selection system can identify when a cheap K-FAC evidence comparison should be trusted, audited, corrected, or abstained from. The main risk is misuse in the opposite direction: an approximate evidence score could be overinterpreted as a definitive Bayesian model-selection result even when the comparison is near a fragile boundary. The proposed mitigation is to report margin information and the Boundary Fragility Score alongside K-FAC evidence scores, and to reserve exact-block or refined-curvature checks for high-BFS comparisons.

Data and ethics. The experiments use synthetic data, public benchmark datasets, and trained-model curvature diagnostics. The manuscript does not introduce human-subjects experiments or a deployed decision system. The main ethical obligation is therefore transparency about scope: the block-level evidence results should not be advertised as full-network marginal-likelihood validation or as a calibrated production detector without additional validation.

AI assistance disclosure. AI tools were used to assist with manuscript evaluation and preparation, as well as code-design discussion. All AI-assisted material, analyses, and code-design choices were reviewed by the authors, who remain responsible for the manuscript’s claims, implementation, and interpretation.

## 13 Future work

The next scientific step should not be another broad grid. The highest-value follow-up is a full-network or multi-block Laplace experiment restricted to near-boundary cases: the pairs where exact evidence margins are small and realized danger is high. That experiment should measure posterior predictive NLL, calibration, and model/prior choices, while testing the conditional amplification hypothesis suggested by the present directionality result: per-block signed evidence bias may amplify rather than cancel when effective-dimension orderings are consistent across layers. The decisive quantities are cross-block sign correlation, cross-layer effective-dimension-ordering correlation, and the growth of the danger ratio as blocks are added. A second follow-up is a deliberately balanced near-tie width-comparison benchmark, because the existing data do not justify a width-dependent Occam-bias claim. A third follow-up is a modern weight-sharing block probe, such as a small attention or transformer-MLP projection block, because modern K-FAC is increasingly used for generic weight-sharing architectures. A fourth follow-up is theoretical: directly decompose saved residual factors by Hermite order to test the rank-growth conjecture suggested by the covariance identity and the aggregate A-side Hermite alignment. A fifth follow-up is algorithmic: turn the K-FAC-side fragility proxy into a calibrated warning rule and design a non-oracle correction that targets differential evidence error, not just Frobenius residual reconstruction.

## 14 Conclusion

K-FAC’s standard factorization is useful, but it discards a specific structured object: the activation–gradient outer-product covariance. That residual is not merely a reconstruction artifact. It affects logdet and effectivedimension quantities used in Laplace evidence, and it can reverse close evidence decisions. The resulting picture is not global failure but boundary fragility. K-FAC is stable when exact evidence margins are large; near decision boundaries, approximation error can exceed the exact margin and change the answer. The Boundary Fragility Score makes this result actionable as a benchmark-local audit signal by flagging many fragile comparisons from K-FAC-side quantities alone; pair-grouped ablations show that the signal is not merely small-margin detection. The directionality result further sharpens the mechanism: the existing data do not support a width-dependent Occam-bias headline, but signed errors robustly penalize higher-effectivedimension candidates. Oracle low-rank residual correction largely repairs the failures, showing that the missing signal is structured. The next algorithmic challenge is to turn this audit signal and oracle repairability into calibrated, robust, scalable residual-aware Laplace evidence tools.
